title: Tess of the d’Urbervilles
author: Thomas Hardy
setting: Hardy’s Wessex: the Vale of Blackmoor, the Var valley, the uplands at Flintcomb-Ash, and Stonehenge
lengthNote: Fifty-nine chapters gathered into seven named phases
openingLine: On an evening in the latter part of May a middle-aged man was walking homeward from Shaston to the village of Marlott, in the adjoining Vale of Blakemore, or Blackmoor.
summary: A parson tells a haggler on a Dorset road that he is descended from knights, and the boast costs his daughter everything. Hardy tracks Tess Durbeyfield through four employers, two men and one dead child, and arranges the novel so that every disaster arrives through ordinary machinery: a horse on a dark road, a letter under a carpet, a threshing engine that will not stop. The subtitle is an argument, and the book is built to win it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Tess of the d’Urbervilles
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously in Roman numerals from I to LIX across the seven phases; references below give the phase as well, since the phases are the divisions Hardy himself named.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Weekly in The Graphic from July to December, cut and altered to suit a family illustrated paper.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Three volumes from James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., with the material the serial had removed restored.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.note: Not a description but a verdict, and the reason much of the first reviewing was about morality rather than the novel.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Hardy names them — The Maiden, Maiden No More, The Rally, The Consequence, The Woman Pays, The Convert, Fulfilment — so that the table of contents reads as a sentence about a life.

structure.label: Phase the First
structure.title: The Maiden
structure.summary: A chance meeting on the road tells John Durbeyfield he is a d’Urberville, and the family’s drunken celebration puts Tess in charge of the horse. Prince is killed, the family loses its living, and Tess is sent to claim kin from a household that bought the name.

scenes.title: The name
scenes.summary: Parson Tringham’s antiquarian civility turns a haggler into a knight, and the club-walking gives Angel Clare his first, unused sight of Tess.

scenes.title: Prince
scenes.summary: Tess takes the beehives to market at night, falls asleep, and the mail-cart kills the horse; the guilt sends her to Trantridge.

scenes.title: The Chase
scenes.summary: Alec installs her in the poultry farm, follows her through the fog after the dance at Chaseborough, and the novel’s central assault is narrated in the dark and in the dark of the prose.

structure.label: Phase the Second
structure.title: Maiden No More
structure.summary: Tess walks home, refuses Alec’s offer of support, and works the harvest with her child at the field edge. Sorrow is baptised by his mother when the parson is refused and buried in the unconsecrated corner with the drunkards and the stillborn.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: She goes back to Marlott and asks her mother why she was never warned.

scenes.title: Sorrow
scenes.summary: The harvest scene, the home baptism, the refused burial, and the two years of silence that follow.

structure.label: Phase the Third
structure.title: The Rally
structure.summary: At Talbothays the work is skilled, the valley is fertile and Tess is briefly an employee rather than a victim. Angel Clare, learning dairying before emigrating, watches her across three months of summer and decides that she is Nature itself, which is the beginning of the trouble.

scenes.title: The Var valley
scenes.summary: A larger landscape, real skill at the milking, and the harp heard across the garden.

scenes.title: Summer
scenes.summary: The dairy’s three other milkmaids love Angel too, and the novel keeps them in view; Angel declares himself in a cart full of milk.

structure.label: Phase the Fourth
structure.title: The Consequence
structure.summary: Tess refuses Angel repeatedly and then accepts, tries four times to tell him, and finally writes it down. The letter goes under the carpet as well as under the door, and the confession she owes is postponed to the wedding night, where he makes his own first.

scenes.title: The engagement
scenes.summary: Angel’s family, his brothers’ respectability, and the ride to the station where Tess begins and abandons her history.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: The note that is never read, the wedding at last, and Angel’s confession of his own forty-eight hours in London.

structure.label: Phase the Fifth
structure.title: The Woman Pays
structure.summary: Angel hears the same offence he has just confessed and finds it a different thing entirely. He leaves for Brazil; Tess sends money home, is turned away from dairy work, and ends at Flintcomb-Ash pulling swedes in the rain and feeding a threshing machine.

scenes.title: The rejection
scenes.summary: The confession, the sleepwalking, the coffin, and the separation dressed as a temporary arrangement.

scenes.title: Flintcomb-Ash
scenes.summary: The starve-acre farm, Marian and Izz, and the walk to Emminster that ends with Tess overhearing the Clare brothers and turning back.

structure.label: Phase the Sixth
structure.title: The Convert
structure.summary: Alec reappears as a ranting preacher and abandons the pulpit within a fortnight of seeing her again, telling her the backsliding is her fault. He follows her to the rick, offers to keep her family, and waits for her father’s death to do the arguing for him.

scenes.title: The preacher
scenes.summary: The conversion, the pursuit across the uplands, and the confrontation on the threshing rick.

scenes.title: Lady Day
scenes.summary: The unanswered letter, John Durbeyfield’s death, the loss of the cottage, and the night in the churchyard at Kingsbere.

structure.label: Phase the Seventh
structure.title: Fulfilment
structure.summary: Angel comes back from Brazil thin and altered, and finds Tess installed in a boarding house at Sandbourne under another man’s protection. She kills Alec, the two of them walk north for five days, and the police take her at dawn on the stone at Stonehenge.

scenes.title: Sandbourne
scenes.summary: The return, the landlady’s staircase, and the spreading stain on the ceiling below.

scenes.title: Stonehenge and Wintoncester
scenes.summary: The empty house in the New Forest, the sleep on the altar stone, the arrest at sunrise, and the black flag over the city gaol.

characters.name: Tess Durbeyfield
characters.role: A field-woman, sixteen at the opening
characters.summary: Hardy gives her the intelligence of a National-school education and the position of an unskilled labourer, and the gap between the two is where the novel lives. She is judged by everyone she meets on evidence she was never allowed to present, and the subtitle exists because Hardy expected his readers to join in.
characters.clue: She baptises her own child with a jug of water because the parson will not come, and names him for a word out of the Bible.

relationships.label: assaulted, pursued and finally killed by her hand

characters.name: Alec d’Urberville
characters.role: Son of a Stoke family that purchased the name
characters.summary: His ancestry is bought and his power is entirely current: money, a gig, a poultry farm, a mother who cannot see. He converts, preaches, relapses and proposes with the same unembarrassed energy, and blames Tess for each turn.
characters.clue: He drives too fast downhill, feeds a girl strawberries she has not asked for, and later preaches in a barn about the sin he committed.

characters.name: Angel Clare
characters.role: A parson’s youngest son, learning farming
characters.summary: He has rejected his father’s church and kept every one of its judgements. The cruelty of the wedding night is not hypocrisy in the ordinary sense — he has genuinely convinced himself that the woman in front of him is a different person from the one he proposed to.
characters.clue: He confesses forty-eight hours of dissipation, is forgiven in a sentence, and cannot manage the same for a confession he has just been given.

characters.name: Joan Durbeyfield
characters.summary: She sends her daughter to claim kin in a clean dress and never explains why a clean dress might matter. Hardy is precise about the gap between them: the mother’s world is ballads and a fortune-telling book, the daughter’s is the Sixth Standard, and two hundred years lie between the two.
characters.clue: She keeps a fortune-telling book in the thatch because she will not have it in the house at night.

characters.name: John Durbeyfield
characters.summary: He is given a title and no money, and spends the rest of his short life being carried home. His death is the event that empties the cottage, because the lease was on his life: the novel’s cruellest joke is that the ancestry which ruined his daughter also fails to house her.
characters.clue: Told on the road that he is descended from knights, he immediately orders a carriage to take him the rest of the way home.

characters.name: Marian
characters.role: A dairymaid at Talbothays, later at Flintcomb-Ash
characters.summary: She loves Angel, loses him without resentment, and is the one who finds Tess work when nobody else will. Her drinking at the starve-acre farm is treated as a fact about the work rather than a fault in her.
characters.clue: The stoutest of the three milkmaids who lie awake listening for a man’s footstep, and the one who later writes to warn of a danger she cannot name.

characters.name: Izz Huett
characters.summary: Asked by Angel to come to Brazil with him, she agrees, and then tells him the truth about how much Tess loved him, which ends the proposal. It is the most disinterested act in the book and nobody thanks her for it.
characters.clue: She is offered a passage to Brazil and talks the man out of it by telling him what another woman would have done for him.

characters.name: Liza-Lu
characters.summary: She is barely characterised until the last pages, when Tess asks Angel to marry her — a request the novel neither endorses nor refuses. She walks away from Wintoncester holding his hand, which is as close to a future as the book offers.
characters.clue: A girl of about sixteen, described as having her sister’s face without her sister’s history, who is handed that history at the end.

themes.name: Purity and the verdict
themes.summary: The subtitle picks a fight before the first page. Hardy’s method is to show the judgement being made — by Angel, by the parson who will not bury Sorrow, by Tess herself — and then to show the evidence on which it rests, which is always somebody else’s conduct.
themes.development: From the refused burial in Phase the Second, through the wedding night in Phase the Fifth, to the narrator’s flat statement that she had broken an accepted social law and no law known to her environment.

themes.name: Class and ancestry
themes.summary: The d’Urberville name is the novel’s original accident: it is worthless as property, potent as fantasy, and purchasable by anyone with money. Hardy sets a family that owns the name legitimately and has nothing against a family that bought it and has everything.
themes.development: Announced on the road in Chapter I, exploited at Trantridge, revived at Kingsbere when the family sleeps under the window of its own vault, and finally irrelevant at the gallows.

themes.name: Work and the land
themes.summary: Nobody in this novel is ever outside the labour market. Tess moves between a poultry farm, a dairy, a swede field and a threshing rick, and each place has its own skills, wages, weather and physical cost, described with the accuracy of someone who had watched it done.
themes.development: The fertile Var valley of Phase the Third is set against the starve-acre uplands of Phase the Fifth, and the threshing machine in Phase the Sixth makes the pace of work no longer human.

themes.name: Chance, timing and cause
themes.summary: A letter slides under a carpet, a horse meets a mail-cart, a man arrives a week too late. Hardy is not arguing that Tess is unlucky; he is arguing that a woman with no money and no standing cannot survive the ordinary accidents that other people absorb.
themes.development: Each phase turns on a small mistimed event, and the narrator repeatedly refuses to call any of them fate while allowing the characters to do so.

themes.name: Religion and its officers
themes.summary: The novel is full of clergy and empty of comfort. A vicar refuses a Christian burial and then privately says it makes no difference; a rake preaches in a barn and abandons it in a fortnight; Angel keeps his father’s morality after discarding his father’s creed.
themes.development: The home baptism in Phase the Second is the book’s one act of genuine sacrament, and it is performed by an unmarried mother in a cottage bedroom.

themes.name: The double standard
themes.summary: Hardy constructs the wedding night as a controlled experiment: two confessions, the same offence, told within an hour of each other, with the sexes reversed. Angel is forgiven in a sentence; the novel then watches him fail to return the favour for the next hundred pages.
themes.development: Set up by the paired confessions in Phase the Fifth, named by the title of that phase, and never retracted — Angel’s eventual forgiveness arrives after it can do any good.

techniques.name: The named phases
techniques.definition: Dividing a novel into large titled units that carry an argument of their own.
techniques.inThisBook: Hardy calls his seven divisions phases rather than books or parts, and names them so that the contents page reads as a sentence: The Maiden, Maiden No More, The Rally, The Consequence, The Woman Pays, The Convert, Fulfilment.

techniques.name: Landscape as pressure
techniques.definition: Using terrain, weather and scale to act on the characters, not to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: The Var valley makes bodies fertile and Flintcomb-Ash makes them cold; the same woman doing the same work is a different creature in each, and Hardy changes his vocabulary accordingly.

techniques.name: Narratorial intervention
techniques.definition: A narrator stepping out of the story to contest the judgement the story is receiving.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator asks where Tess’s guardian angel was, declares that she had broken no law known to her surroundings, and closes with a sentence about the President of the Immortals that is deliberately unfair to the universe.

techniques.name: Machinery
techniques.definition: Industrial equipment introduced into a rural setting as an agent in the plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The threshing machine at Flintcomb-Ash sets the tempo of a whole chapter: the engineer is described as a stranger from another world, and Tess cannot leave the platform while it runs.

techniques.name: Dialect and register
techniques.definition: Marking class and education through the grammar characters are given.
techniques.inThisBook: Tess speaks two languages — the dialect at home and ordinary English at school and abroad — and Hardy says so explicitly, which makes the gap between her and her mother measurable in sentences.

techniques.name: Omens and retrospect
techniques.definition: Planting details whose significance is only available on a second reading.
techniques.inThisBook: The cock that crows in the afternoon, the d’Urberville coach, the blood on the ceiling at Sandbourne: the superstitions belong to the characters, and the patterning belongs to Hardy.

quotations.text: Then what might your meaning be in calling me ‘Sir John’ these different times, when I be plain Jack Durbeyfield, the haggler?
quotations.speaker: John Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the road to Marlott, to Parson Tringham, who has greeted him by a title.
quotations.analysis: He states his own name and trade accurately and in dialect, and it is the last time in the book anyone does so without embarrassment. The sentence is the hinge of the whole plot: a man asks for an explanation of a courtesy, and is given an ancestry he cannot afford.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter I

quotations.text: ’Tis because we be on a blighted star, and not a sound one, isn’t it, Tess?
quotations.speaker: Abraham Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the cart on the road to Casterbridge, after Tess has explained the stars to him, and before the mail-cart kills the horse.
quotations.analysis: A child converts an astronomy lesson into a theory of his family’s luck, and the novel lets it stand as the best available explanation. The image is agricultural rather than cosmic — the blighted apple on the stubbard-tree — so the cosmology is made out of the only materials the Durbeyfields have.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter IV

quotations.text: might some say, where was Tess’s guardian angel? where was the providence of her simple faith? Perhaps, like that other god of whom the ironical Tishbite spoke, he was talking, or he was pursuing, or he was in a journey, or he was sleeping and not to be awaked.
quotations.context: In The Chase, at the moment the narrative declines to describe.
quotations.analysis: The question is put into the mouth of an imagined objector — ‘might some say’ — so that the narrator can ask it without quite owning it. The answer comes from Elijah mocking the priests of Baal, which turns a plea for providence into a joke about a god who is out of the office.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: Why it was that upon this beautiful feminine tissue, sensitive as gossamer, and practically blank as snow as yet, there should have been traced such a coarse pattern as it was doomed to receive; why so often the coarse appropriates the finer thus, the wrong man the woman, the wrong woman the man, many thousand years of analytical philosophy have failed to explain to our sense of order.
quotations.context: Immediately after the assault, in the narrator’s own voice.
quotations.analysis: Tess is described as fabric and the assault as a pattern traced on it, which keeps the violence entirely out of the grammar: there is no assailant in the sentence, only a coarseness that appropriates a fineness. The evasion has been read both as Hardy’s delicacy and as his failure of nerve.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: An immeasurable social chasm was to divide our heroine’s personality thereafter from that previous self of hers who stepped from her mother’s door to try her fortune at Trantridge poultry-farm.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the first phase.
quotations.analysis: The damage is described as social rather than personal: what has changed is not Tess but the distance between two versions of her, and the chasm is measured from her mother’s door to a poultry farm. Hardy ends the phase on a job title, which is where the novel always puts its weight.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: How could I be expected to know? I was a child when I left this house four months ago. Why didn’t you tell me there was danger in menfolk? Why didn’t you warn me? Ladies know what to fend hands against, because they read novels that tell them of these tricks; but I never had the chance o’ learning in that way, and you did not help me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Back at Marlott, answering her mother’s complaint that she has not managed to get Alec to marry her.
quotations.analysis: The accusation is about information, not morality: ladies read novels and therefore know, and Tess had no access to the warning. It is the only moment in the book where she names the mechanism of her own ruin, and she names it as a class fact.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XII

quotations.text: But all the while she was making a distinction where there was no difference. Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord. She had been made to break an accepted social law, but no law known to the environment in which she fancied herself such an anomaly.
quotations.context: Walking at night after her return, believing herself a figure of guilt among innocent birds and hedges.
quotations.analysis: The sentence performs a small legal argument: there is an accepted social law and there is the law of the environment, and only the first has been broken. ‘Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord’ inverts her self-accusation without arguing with it, which is Hardy’s usual method of defence.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: Sorrow, I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the bedroom at Marlott, at one in the morning, her father having locked the door against the parson.
quotations.analysis: She uses the exact liturgical formula, which is why the vicar afterwards cannot say the rite was invalid — only that it will not buy a place in the churchyard. The child’s name is a common noun, so the sentence baptises an emotion, and the form of words is the one piece of institutional authority Tess is able to take for herself.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIV

quotations.text: So passed away Sorrow the Undesired⁠—that intrusive creature, that bastard gift of shameless Nature, who respects not the social law
quotations.context: After the burial in the corner of the churchyard reserved for the unbaptised and the suicides.
quotations.analysis: Three epithets in one clause, each in a different voice: the mother’s, the parish’s and the narrator’s. ‘Shameless Nature, who respects not the social law’ sets the two jurisdictions of the whole novel against each other in eight words, and leaves no doubt which one Hardy thinks is real.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIV

quotations.text: The world was drawn to a larger pattern here. The enclosures numbered fifty acres instead of ten
quotations.context: Tess’s first sight of the Var valley from the ridge, on the way to Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: The change of scene is registered as a change of measurement: fields, herds and horizons all get bigger, and so does the room she has to move in. Hardy is careful to make the relief agricultural — this is better land, and better land means steadier work.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Third, Chapter XVI

quotations.text: What a fresh and virginal daughter of Nature that milkmaid is!
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Angel identifying the new milkmaid, to himself, at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Every word of it is a category rather than a person, and two of them will be used against her within a year. He is not lying and he is not looking: the sentence is a piece of pastoral criticism applied to a colleague, and the novel records that he said it to himself.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Third, Chapter XVIII

quotations.text: There was hardly a touch of earth in her love for Clare. To her sublime trustfulness he was all that goodness could be⁠—knew all that a guide, philosopher, and friend should know. She thought every line in the contour of his person the perfection of masculine beauty, his soul the soul of a saint, his intellect that of a seer.
quotations.context: During the engagement at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Her love is described as having no earth in it, in a book where earth is the one thing that can be relied on. The triple structure — guide, philosopher and friend, then saint and seer — makes her devotion sound liturgical, and prepares the exact ground on which he will later refuse her.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fourth, Chapter XXXI

quotations.text: under the edge of the carpet she discerned the faint white margin of the envelope containing her letter to him, which he obviously had never seen, owing to her having in her haste thrust it beneath the carpet as well as beneath the door.
quotations.context: The morning of the wedding, in the room where Angel has been sleeping.
quotations.analysis: The disaster is a matter of half an inch of floor covering, and Hardy makes the reader watch her find it rather than reporting it afterwards. Note that the sentence assigns the error to her haste, not to malice or fate: the novel’s catastrophes are almost always this small and this domestic.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fourth, Chapter XXXIII

quotations.text: I repeat, the woman I have been loving is not you.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: At the old d’Urberville farmhouse, hours after his own confession has been forgiven.
quotations.analysis: ‘I repeat’ tells us he has already said it once, which is the cruellest word in the sentence. He does not accuse her of anything; he unmakes her, replacing a person with a category error, and the novel has spent a whole phase showing that the category was his invention.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fifth, Chapter XXXV

quotations.text: How can we live together while that man lives?⁠—he being your husband in nature, and not I.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Refusing Tess’s plea to be allowed to stay with him as a servant if not as a wife.
quotations.analysis: He converts an assault into a marriage and then reasons from it: the man who forced her is ‘your husband in nature’. The argument is legal in shape and biological in content, and it is the clearest statement in the book of the belief the subtitle was written to attack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fifth, Chapter XXXVI

quotations.text: Close under the eaves of the stack, and as yet barely visible, was the red tyrant that the women had come to serve⁠—a timber-framed construction, with straps and wheels appertaining⁠—the threshing-machine which, whilst it was going, kept up a despotic demand upon the endurance of their muscles and nerves.
quotations.context: Dawn at Flintcomb-Ash, as the threshing gang assembles.
quotations.analysis: The machine is given a colour, a title and a household of servants before it is given a technical description. ‘Despotic demand’ converts a wage relationship into a political one, and the women are the last link in it: the engine sets the speed, and Tess cannot step off the platform while it runs.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: Whip me, crush me; you need not mind those people under the rick! I shall not cry out. Once victim, always victim⁠—that’s the law!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the threshing rick, after striking Alec across the mouth with her leather glove.
quotations.analysis: She invites the punishment and states the principle in the same breath, and the word she chooses is ‘law’. It is the same word the narrator used in Phase the Second about the accepted social law she had broken, and here Tess speaks it as if it were physics.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: Remember, my lady, I was your master once! I will be your master again. If you are any man’s wife you are mine!
quotations.speaker: Alec d’Urberville
quotations.context: Holding her by the shoulders on the rick, after she has refused his offer to keep her family.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three tenses: was, will be, are. The vocabulary is of ownership throughout, and ‘my lady’ is a sneer at the ancestry that brought her to him in the first place. The threat is also a prediction, and the novel lets it come true.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: I must cry to you in my trouble⁠—I have no one else! I am so exposed to temptation, Angel. I fear to say who it is, and I do not like to write about it at all. But I cling to you in a way you cannot think! Can you not come to me now, at once, before anything terrible happens?
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: The letter written at Flintcomb-Ash and sent to Angel’s parents to be forwarded to Brazil.
quotations.analysis: She will not name the danger even in a private letter, which is exactly the reticence that has cost her twice already. The phrase ‘before anything terrible happens’ is the novel’s only piece of accurate forecasting, and the distance to Brazil guarantees that it arrives too late to be one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVIII

quotations.text: Angel, I am almost glad⁠—yes, glad! This happiness could not have lasted. It was too much. I have had enough; and now I shall not live for you to despise me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Waking on the stone at Stonehenge as the police close in at dawn.
quotations.analysis: Her last argument is about time rather than justice: the happiness was too much, so it could not have lasted, so ending it now is a form of thrift. ‘I shall not live for you to despise me’ shows that the wedding night is still the governing event of her life, five years and two men later.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Seventh, Chapter LVIII

quotations.text: the President of the Immortals, in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess.
quotations.context: As the black flag rises over Wintoncester gaol and Angel and Liza-Lu watch from the hill.
quotations.analysis: Hardy puts ‘Justice’ in quotation marks and then hands the credit to a figure out of Aeschylus, which lets him blame a god he does not believe in for a sentence passed by an English court. The evasion is deliberate: no judge, no juror and no clergyman is named, and the reader is left to supply them.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Seventh, Chapter LIX

timeline.label: Thomas Hardy born at Higher Bockhampton
timeline.detail: In a cottage on the edge of the heath, three miles from Dorchester, into a family of builders and masons.

timeline.label: The Elementary Education Act
timeline.detail: The schooling that gives Tess her Sixth Standard English and opens the two-hundred-year gap Hardy describes between her and her mother.

timeline.label: Far from the Madding Crowd
timeline.detail: The novel that made Hardy’s name and fixed Wessex as a place readers expected to revisit.

timeline.label: The Mayor of Casterbridge
timeline.detail: Dorchester under its Wessex name, and the same interest in a man ruined by a single early act.

timeline.label: Serialised in The Graphic
timeline.detail: Weekly from July to December, with the seduction, the baptism and other material cut or altered for a family illustrated paper.

timeline.label: First book edition
timeline.detail: Three volumes from James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., restoring the excised material and carrying the subtitle A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented.

timeline.label: One-volume edition
timeline.detail: A cheaper single volume widens the readership, and Hardy goes on revising the text in later issues.

timeline.label: Jude the Obscure
timeline.detail: The reception of Hardy’s last novel effectively ended his career as a novelist; he wrote poetry for the next thirty years.

timeline.label: Lorimer Stoddard’s stage version opens in New York
timeline.detail: Minnie Maddern Fiske played Tess from 2 March, and made the part a major role in the American theatre.

timeline.label: Silent film with Blanche Sweet
timeline.detail: Blanche Sweet as Tess, Stuart Holmes as Alec and Conrad Nagel as Angel; the film is now considered lost.

timeline.label: Hardy dies
timeline.detail: His ashes were buried in Westminster Abbey and his heart at Stinsford, which is the most Hardyan fact about him.

timeline.label: Roman Polanski’s Tess
timeline.detail: Nastassja Kinski in the title role; the film won Academy Awards for cinematography, art direction and costume design.

timeline.label: BBC four-part adaptation
timeline.detail: Written by David Nicholls and directed by David Blair, with Gemma Arterton as Tess.

places.name: Marnhull, Dorset
places.note: Hardy’s Marlott, in the Vale of Blackmoor: the club-walking, the cottage, and the night journey with the beehives.

places.name: Cranborne Chase
places.note: The Chase, the oldest wood in England in Hardy’s description, and the place the novel refuses to describe.

places.name: Dorchester

criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats Tess as a modern tragic heroine destroyed by forces larger than herself — heredity, chance, the decay of the rural economy — with the President of the Immortals as the novel’s own summary of the case.
criticalViews.counter: It risks letting Alec and Angel off as instruments of fate, when the book is careful to show each of them choosing, at leisure, what to do next.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the work has read the book as a record of the late-Victorian agricultural labour market: the annual hirings, the loss of lifehold cottages, the arrival of steam threshing, and what all of that does to a woman without a settlement.
criticalViews.counter: Read only this way, the marriage plot becomes an interruption, and the novel’s very deliberate arguments about purity and judgement go unanswered.

criticalViews.position: A novel about who is allowed to speak
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism, particularly feminist criticism from the 1970s onwards, has focused on the narration itself: Tess is described, painted, watched and argued over, and the scene on which everything turns is narrated in her absence from the prose.
criticalViews.counter: Hardy’s defenders point out that the same narrator is the only voice in the book that consistently argues on her side, and that the subtitle cost him a great deal.

essayQuestions.question: How does Hardy use the seven phases to shape the reader’s judgement of Tess?
plan: Set out the titles in order and show that they form a narrative sentence about a life rather than a list of parts.
Contrast The Maiden and Maiden No More: the second title is imposed by other people, and the phase opens with Tess walking home.
Use The Rally to show Hardy granting a recovery that the structure has already told us is temporary.
Read The Woman Pays as the book’s thesis statement, and check it against the paired confessions that open the phase.
Weigh Fulfilment: an ironic title, a religious one, or an accurate description of what Tess says on the stone at Stonehenge.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Tess is destroyed by circumstance, not by character.’ Discuss.
plan: List the accidents: the mail-cart, the letter under the carpet, the Clare brothers on the road, Angel’s return a few weeks late.
Show that each one is small, domestic and survivable by somebody with money — and that Hardy makes that point rather than the reader.
Set against this the decisions actually taken: Alec at Trantridge, Angel on the wedding night, Joan Durbeyfield sending her daughter to claim kin.
Examine the narrator’s own interventions, which repeatedly refuse fate as an explanation while allowing the characters to reach for it.
Test the last paragraph: does the President of the Immortals settle the question or dodge it?

essayQuestions.question: Examine Hardy’s presentation of work in the novel.
plan: Start with the fact that Tess is always employed, and track the four workplaces in order: Trantridge, Talbothays, Flintcomb-Ash, Sandbourne.
Show how the prose changes with the land — the Var valley’s abundance against the flint uplands’ grey, and how each is described through the body doing the work.
Read the threshing scene closely: the machine’s tempo, the engineer as a stranger, and the fact that Tess cannot leave the platform.
Connect labour to power: every one of Alec’s advantages is contractual, from the poultry farm to the offer to keep her family.
Conclude on Lady Day and the lost cottage, where a lifehold agreement does more damage than either man.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the novel earn its subtitle?
plan: Establish what the subtitle claims and whom it is addressed to: not Tess, but the readers who will judge her.
Use the refused burial and the home baptism to show institutions and individuals reaching opposite verdicts on the same child.
Read the wedding night as a controlled experiment in the double standard, with the same offence confessed twice in an hour.
Consider the cost of the defence: Tess is repeatedly described rather than heard, and the assault itself happens outside the prose.
Decide whether Hardy’s narrator persuades or merely insists, and whether the last sentence helps or weakens the case.

discussionQuestions: Hardy does not describe what happens in The Chase. Is that restraint, evasion, or a way of making the reader supply the verdict?
Angel confesses first and is forgiven in a sentence. What would the novel lose if that order were reversed?
The letter goes under the carpet as well as under the door. Does that small accident convince you, or does it feel arranged?
Alec’s conversion lasts a fortnight. Is the novel attacking religion, or attacking him?
Tess asks Angel to marry her sister. What is being offered, and what is being taken away?

related.why: Another dependent woman whose employer’s household turns out to hold a prior claim, and who walks out of it onto the moor with nothing.
A community’s verdict on an unmarried mother, and a child named for the circumstances of her birth.
Published eight years later, and equally interested in what a woman is permitted to want once the marriage is in place.
A life reorganised around a fantasy of gentility, and a fortune whose real source is nothing like the imagined one.
Landscape as an agent rather than a setting, and a plot in which class humiliation is passed down a generation.
